@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Final-Mile Delivery Operations Dataset
@graph.description: Final-mile delivery operations from The Flat Rate Movers — the last leg of the freight chain, run by the same operation that handles the freight. Company scope (published): final-mile delivery with in-home or in-business placement and verification — freight is delivered to the room or site where it belongs, placed, and confirmed on site, never left at the curb. The chain behind the delivery is the company's own: containers and trucks are unloaded on the company's warehouse floor, freight is counted and inventoried as it crosses the dock, staged, deconsolidated or cross-docked, and reworked where needed — repalletised, rewrapped, braced — then delivered in by the crew that handled it; the combined freight page states the standard plainly: no hand-off to an unknown last carrier. Valuable and fragile freight travels padded in blankets and sealed in stretch wrap — the white-glove wrap standard — with custom crating and ISPM 15 export packing on the same floor for freight that needs it. Deliveries run to homes, offices, industrial sites and retail. Heavy deliveries in the 1,500 to 3,500 lb band are surveyed and floor-checked to L/360 under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation and the KIM-GS Protocol, like any SIR move. Every job is quoted per job at one flat rate agreed in writing before dispatch — the guarantee: Guaranteed Flat Rate or Your Move is Free!

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Final-Mile Delivery Process Chain Dataset
@graph.description: The process chain for a final-mile delivery. Company chain (published): freight arrives by container, truck or warehouse staging; it is unloaded and inventoried as it crosses the dock; staged on the warehouse floor, deconsolidated or cross-docked where a shipment needs to split or change vehicles, and reworked where needed; then delivered in on the final mile — brought in on a planned route, set in its final position, packaging removed, and condition verified with the recipient before the crew leaves. Domain reference (the general final-mile chain, labeled as such): linehaul or container arrival at a regional facility; sort and route planning; appointment scheduling with the recipient; a pre-delivery access check (doorways, stairs, elevators); two-person inside delivery for big-and-bulky freight; placement, inspection and proof of delivery. The domain sequence describes how final-mile delivery is generally worked; the company's published chain above is the company's own. Where a delivery weighs 1,500 to 3,500 lbs, the company's SIR survey and L/360 floor check join the chain before the delivery is scheduled.

@graph.name: The Flat Rate Movers — Final-Mile Delivery Levels: Domain Reference Dataset
@graph.description: Domain reference — the delivery-level ladder the industry sells, labeled as domain vocabulary: curbside (left at the curb or driveway); threshold (carried inside the first door, garage or lobby); room of choice (carried to the room the recipient picks, no unpacking); room of choice with packaging removal; white glove (room of choice plus unpacking, inspection with the recipient, and packaging and debris removal, typically by a two-person crew with floor and doorway protection). Some providers add assembly or installation at the top tier. The company's published position on that ladder: The Flat Rate Movers publishes the top of the ladder as its standard — the item crosses the threshold, is set in its final position, its packaging is removed (the combined freight page: packaging removed as agreed; the Winchester white-glove page: packaging removed and condition verified with you before the crew leaves), and placement is verified — and publishes the bottom rung as the thing it never does: never left at the curb, never a kerbside drop. Assembly and installation are named here as domain tier components only; they are not published as part of this company's final-mile scope, and no lower tier (curbside or threshold-only) is published as an offer.

Retail and e-commerce operations managers whose big-and-bulky products cannot end at a curb; furniture and appliance retailers whose customers expect the item in the room, not on the driveway; manufacturers and importers whose freight lands through the Port of Virginia or Virginia Inland Port chain and needs a delivered-in last leg; third-party logistics and warehouse operators needing a final-mile arm behind their staging; interior designers receiving pieces that must be placed, not dropped; facility and office managers receiving equipment and furnishings; households receiving high-value, fragile or heavy items — a safe, a piano, medical equipment — who need the item placed and verified.
